response.query: How can simultaneous multi-contact interactions be written as a single LCP or sequence of LCPs that encode no-penetration, Coulomb friction cones, and energy-dissipative impacts while remaining computationally tractable?
response.answer: Simultaneous multi-contact interactions can be modeled using a sequence of time-varying linear complementarity problems (LCPs) that encode no-penetration, Coulomb friction, and energy-dissipative impacts. Efficient solvers and pre-computation techniques ensure computational tractability.

results.title: Fast Contact-Implicit Model Predictive Control
results.content: Contact-implicit model predictive control (CI-MPC) generalizes linear MPC to contact-rich settings by utilizing a bi-level planning formulation with lower-level contact dynamics formulated as time-varying linear complementarity problems (LCPs) computed using strategic Taylor approximations about a reference trajectory. To enable real-time performance for control, we pre-compute linearizations of the system’s dynamics, signed-distance functions, and friction cones about a reference tra-jectory, while explicitly retaining complementarity constraints that encode contact switching behavior, resulting in a sequence of lower-level time-varying linear-complementarity problems (LCP) which represent the model’s contact dynamics. Our contributions are: • Fast approximate contact dynamics that can be reliably evaluated and efﬁciently differentiated with a custom interior-point solver • Structure-exploiting solvers for the contact-dynamics and trajectory optimization problems • A model predictive control framework for robotic systems with contact dynamics • A collection of simulation and hardware experiments demonstrating the performance of CI-MPC on a variety of robotic systems across a range of highly dynamic tasks In the remainder of this paper, we ﬁrst review related work on control through contact with MPC, as well as complementarity-based contact dynamics in Section II. Dissipation mechanisms and dissipative forces play a pivotal role in the operations and performance of human-machine interfaces and particularly in haptic systems. Coulomb friction in general can be the most influential element in systems involving multiple direct contact connections such as joints with transmissions or mechanically guided components. The effect of Coulomb friction is often neglected in haptics. The part of the literature which deals with friction mainly focuses on friction compensation and/or simulation of friction for haptic rendering. In this paper, the nature of the dynamic behavior caused by Coulomb friction in haptic sampled-data systems is illustrated by experiment, analysis, and simulation. It is also demonstrated that a simple model can represent this behavior and show the effects of the haptic system parameters on this dynamics.
